dublinCore.description: An interactive choropleth map that grades each of the 50 US states on 8 quality of life metrics: personal income, poverty rate, education attainment, life expectancy, infant mortality, violent crime, median home price and food insecurity. A state's color shows how many of the 8 metrics are better than the national average, from dark green (8 of 8) to dark red (0 of 8). Hovering over a state lists its 8 values with a + or - for each, and clicking a state zooms the map to it.
dublinCore.source: State values in data.json, attributed there to the Bureau of Economic Analysis, US Census Bureau, CDC National Center for Health Statistics, FBI Uniform Crime Report, Zillow Home Value Index and USDA Economic Research Service

searchKeywords: quality of life by state map

learningObjectives: Interpret the color of a state on a choropleth map as the number of metrics on which the state is better than the national average.
Explain why a higher value is better for income, education and life expectancy, while a lower value is better for poverty, infant mortality, violent crime, home price and food insecurity.
Compare two states metric by metric to find which metrics account for the difference in their grades.
Evaluate the limits of an index that gives every metric equal weight and counts only whether a value is better or worse than average.
prerequisites: Locating US states on a map
Percentages and rates such as per 1,000 and per 100,000

misconceptions.misconception: A state with high personal income has a high quality of life grade.
misconceptions.correction: Income is one of 8 equally weighted metrics, so a state can beat the average on income and still fall below it on most of the others.
misconceptions.evidence: Texas has a personal income of $56,890, above the $55,000 average, yet its grade is 2/8.

misconceptions.misconception: Low home prices mean a high grade, and high home prices mean a low grade.
misconceptions.correction: Median home price counts as a single metric. The other 7 metrics decide most of the grade.
misconceptions.evidence: Massachusetts has a median home price of $595,000 and a grade of 7/8, while Alabama has a median home price of $232,000 and a grade of 1/8.

misconceptions.misconception: A state graded 0/8 is far worse than average on every metric.
misconceptions.correction: The grade counts how many metrics are worse than average and ignores how much worse each one is.
misconceptions.evidence: Alaska is graded 0/8, yet its median home price ($359,000 against $350,000) and its food insecurity rate (10.8% against 10.5%) are close to the national averages.

dependencies: US state boundaries GeoJSON (PublicaMundi/MappingAPI on raw.githubusercontent.com)
data.json (local file with the state metrics and national averages)

inputSources: data.json: 8 metric values and ranks for each state, the national averages, and a higher-is-better flag for each metric
us-states.json: GeoJSON state boundaries fetched from GitHub
OpenStreetMap tile server: base map tiles
User: pointer hover, click, drag and scroll wheel
dataProcessing: Compare each metric value of a state with the national average, using the higher-is-better flag to set the direction
Count the metrics that are better than average to give a grade from 0 to 8
Look up the label and the fill color for the grade
outputTargets: Fill color of each state shape on the map
Info panel listing the 8 metrics of the hovered state

accessibility.screenReaderScript: A map of the United States in which each of the 50 states is filled with one of nine colors. The color shows how many of 8 quality of life metrics are better than the national average, from dark green for 8 of 8 through yellow for 4 of 8 to dark red for 0 of 8. Hovering over a state opens a panel with the state's name, its grade, and a row for each metric giving the rank, the value, and a plus sign if the value is better than average or a minus sign if it is worse. A legend below the map lists the nine colors.

colorScheme.accent: #1a5e1a to #8B0000 (nine-step green to red grade scale)

controls.label: State shapes on the map
controls.description: Each of the 50 state shapes responds to the pointer. Hovering outlines the state and lists its 8 metrics in the info panel; clicking zooms the map to the state.

properties.action: highlightFeature on hover, resetHighlight on leave, zoomToFeature on click

controls.label: Zoom in
controls.description: The Leaflet + button at the top left of the map zooms in one level.

controls.label: Zoom out
controls.description: The Leaflet - button at the top left of the map zooms out one level.

visualElements.description: A 420-pixel-high Leaflet map with a choropleth of the 50 states over OpenStreetMap tiles. Each state is filled with one of nine grade colors. The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico have no data and are filled gray. The map can also be dragged and zoomed with the scroll wheel.

An info panel in a top corner of the map shows the hovered state's name, abbreviation, grade badge and counts of better and worse metrics, then one row per metric with its rank, value and a green + or red -. The panel moves to the top left for states east of 100 degrees west longitude so that it does not cover the state.
A legend below the map with nine color swatches labeled from 8/8 Best through 4/8 Avg to 0/8 Worst.
A title and subtitle above the map and the instruction 'Hover over a state to see detailed metrics' below the legend.

model.description: Each state is compared with the national average on 8 metrics. The grade is the number of metrics on which the state is better than average, and the grade sets the state's color.
equations: better = value > national average, for metrics where higher is better (personal income, education attainment, life expectancy)
better = value < national average, for metrics where lower is better (poverty rate, infant mortality, violent crime, median home price, food insecurity)
grade = number of the 8 metrics that are better (0 to 8)
assumptions: The national averages are fixed reference values stored in data.json and are not computed from the 50 state values
A state average describes the whole state
limitations: A value equal to the national average counts as worse; this affects 11 of the 400 state metric values, including three for Maine
The grade ignores how far a value is from the average

The rank shown beside each metric is read from data.json and is not computed from the values; some ranks disagree with the values (North Dakota has the highest personal income but is ranked 5, and two states are ranked 1 for median home price)
The District of Columbia and Puerto Rico are drawn on the map but have no data
State averages hide differences within a state, such as urban and rural areas
The data describe 2023-2024 and do not update

variables.name: personalIncome
variables.description: Per capita personal income adjusted for regional cost of living. Higher is better. National average: 55000

variables.name: povertyRate
variables.description: Percentage of the population below the poverty line, adjusted for regional differences. Lower is better. National average: 11.5

variables.name: educationAttainment
variables.description: Percentage of adults aged 25 and over with a bachelor's degree or higher. Higher is better. National average: 33.0

variables.name: lifeExpectancy
variables.description: Average life expectancy at birth. Higher is better. National average: 77.5

variables.name: infantMortality
variables.description: Deaths under 1 year of age. Lower is better. National average: 5.5

variables.name: violentCrime
variables.description: Violent crimes. Lower is better. National average: 380

variables.name: medianHomePrice
variables.description: Median listing price for homes. Lower is better. National average: 350000

variables.name: foodInsecurity
variables.description: Percentage of households experiencing food insecurity. Lower is better. National average: 10.5

variables.name: betterCount
variables.description: The grade: the number of metrics on which the state is better than the national average

variables.name: color
variables.description: The fill color of the state, looked up from the grade in a nine-color scale

scenarios.name: best-grade
scenarios.description: Minnesota is the only state better than the national average on all 8 metrics (8/8, dark green)

scenarios.name: worst-grade
scenarios.description: Alaska and Nevada are worse than the national average on all 8 metrics (0/8, dark red)

scenarios.name: high-income-low-grade
scenarios.description: Texas beats the average on personal income and median home price only (2/8)

scenarios.name: expensive-homes-high-grade
scenarios.description: Massachusetts beats the average on every metric except median home price (7/8)

instructionalStrategies: Predict, then test: students guess their own state's grade and the metrics it is better on before hovering over it
Pair comparison: each pair picks two neighboring states with different colors and lists the metrics that explain the difference
Index critique: students propose a different weighting or a different set of metrics and argue how the map would change

assessmentQuestions.question: Which state is better than the national average on all 8 metrics?
For which of the 8 metrics is a lower value better, and why?
Texas has above-average personal income but a grade of 2/8. Which metrics lower its grade?
Alaska and Nevada are both graded 0/8. Does that mean they are equally far below average? Use their metric values to support your answer.

extensions: Add a control that colors the map by a single metric
Replace the better-or-worse count with a weighted score that uses the distance from the average
Recompute the ranks from the values instead of reading them from data.json
Add metrics such as air quality or commute time
